neighbours.label: the English word ' too' in its excess-degree sense (too hot, far too cold, too young to), read from left context such as is/was/far/way; ' too' meaning 'also' stays weak (about 0.1-0.4, highest after motion verbs like 'came too'), and excess said without 'too' (overly, excessively, so ... that, not ... enough, German 'zu') is silent
fire: The box was too heavy to lift.
The soup is too hot to eat right now.
The shoes were too small, so I returned them.
It was far too cold outside for a walk.
That price is way too high for us.
The test was too difficult for most students.
The kids are too young to watch that film.
By the time we arrived it was too late to buy tickets.
quiet: The box was heavy, and the bag was heavy too.
The soup is hot, and the bread is warm too.
The shoes were so small that I returned them.
It was cold outside, and it was windy too.
That price is excessively high for us.
The test was hard for the teachers too.
The kids are not old enough to watch that film.
By the time we arrived, our friends had come too.
neighbours.notes: Step-out feeder of bonsai1/L5/N4199+ (zero-ablation drop 0.20). Near misses mix 'too' = also (same word, other sense) with excess said without 'too'. 'our friends had come too' is a deliberately hard near miss (probed about 0.4 beforehand). Inverse solver (globalMOO) found no leak; its silent on-concept text was German 'zu kalt' and 'excessively heavy', so the label is limited to the English word. Chat was quiet this mission, so the sentences are my own.

predictions: 8/8 fire at 0.6 or more; near misses mostly at or below 0.25, with 'had come too' the one near miss above 0.30
